And in those days Tharmuth, the daughter of Pharaoh, came to bathe in the river, and she heard your voice crying, and she told her maidens to bring you forth, and they brought you to her. (47:5).
And she took you out of the ark, and she had compassion on you. (47:6).
And your sister said to her: 'Shall I go and call to you one of the Hebrew women to nurse and suckle this babe for you?' (47:7).
And she said <to her>: 'Go.' And she went and called your mother Jochebed, and she gave her wages, and she nursed you. (47:8).

And afterwards, when you wast grown up, they brought you to the daughter of Pharaoh, and you didst become her son, and Amram your father taught you writing, and after you hadst completed three weeks they brought you into the royal court. (47:9).

And you wast three weeks of years at court until the time [2351-] when you didst go forth from the royal court and didst see an Egyptian smiting your friend who was [2372 A.M.] of the children of Israel, and you didst slay him and hide him in the sand. (47:10).
And on the second day you didst and two of the children of Israel striving together, and you didst say to him who was doing the wrong: 'Why do you smite your brother?' (47:11).

And he was angry and indignant, and said: 'Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Thinkest you to kill me as you killedst the Egyptian yesterday?' And you didst fear and flee on account of these words. (47:12).
crossRefs: Exodus 1:15-22: Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives to kill the boys at birth, and when they refuse he commands all his people to cast every son into the river.
Exodus 2:1-10: The child is hidden three months, set in an ark of bulrushes daubed with slime and pitch among the reeds, taken up by Pharaoh's daughter, and nursed by his own mother for wages.
Exodus 6:20: Amram took Jochebed his father's sister to wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, the parents this chapter names.
Acts 7:20-29: Stephen gives Moses forty years in Egypt, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, before he strikes the Egyptian down and flees.
Hebrews 11:23-27: By faith Moses was hidden three months by his parents because they saw he was a fair child and did not fear the king's commandment.

translationNotes.note: Tevah names exactly two objects in the Hebrew Bible: Noah's vessel at Genesis 6:14 and the basket for Moses at Exodus 2:3. Both are sealed with pitch and both carry the one who comes through the water alive. At 47:4 the book gives the same two sealants, pitch and asphalt.

translationNotes.term: Three weeks of years at court
translationNotes.note: At 47:9-10 Moses is handed to Pharaoh's daughter, taught writing by Amram, and brought into the royal court after three weeks, where he stays three weeks of years, which is twenty-one years on this book's reckoning. Acts 7:23 has him forty years old when he goes out to his brothers, and Exodus 7:7 has him eighty when he stands before Pharaoh.

Exodus 2:5-10 leaves Pharaoh's daughter unnamed; at 47:5 this book calls her Tharmuth. The mother is named Jochebed at Exodus 6:20. Paying a Hebrew woman wages to nurse the child is the whole point of Miriam's question, since the boy goes straight back to his own mother with the palace paying for his keep.

Suf is the reed or papyrus growing in the shallows, and Exodus 2:3 places the basket in it. The same word names the sea Israel crosses, yam suf, the sea of reeds, at Exodus 15:4. Bundled and pitched papyrus was a real boat-building material in Egypt, which Isaiah 18:2 mentions as vessels of bulrushes upon the waters.

stories.keyTakeaway: Pharaoh orders the male children thrown into the river, and Moses is born in the seventh month of that order. His mother hides him three months, then sets him in a pitched ark among the reeds where Miriam guards him. Pharaoh's daughter takes him up and his own mother nurses him for wages.

stories.title: 📜 Jubilees 48
summaryBullets: And in the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee you didst depart and dwell <in [2372 A.M.] the land of Midian>, five weeks and one year. And you didst return into Egypt in the second week in the second year in the fiftieth jubilee. (48:1).

And you yourself know what He spoke to you on [2410 A.M.] Mount Sinai, and what prince Mastêmâ desired to do with you when you wast returning into Egypt <on the way when you didst meet him at the lodging-place>. (48:2).
Did he not with all his power seek to slay you and deliver the Egyptians out of your hand when he saw that you wast sent to execute judgment and vengeance on the Egyptians? (48:3).

And I delivered you out of his hand, and you didst perform the signs and wonders which you wast sent to perform in Egypt against Pharaoh, and against all his house, and against his servants and his people. (48:4).

And the Lord executed a great vengeance on them for Israel's sake, and smote them through (the plagues of) blood and frogs, lice and dog-flies, and malignant boils breaking forth in blains; and their cattle by death; and by hail-stones, thereby He destroyed everything that grew for them; and by locusts which devoured the residue which had been left by the hail, and by darkness; and <by the death> of the first-born of men and animals, and on all their idols the Lord took vengeance and burned them with fire. (48:5).

And everything was sent through your hand, that you should declare (these things) before they were done, and you didst speak with the king of Egypt before all his servants and before his people. (48:6).
And everything took place according to your words; ten great and terrible judgments came on the land of Egypt that you mightest execute vengeance on it for Israel. (48:7).

And the Lord did everything for Israel's sake, and according to His covenant, which he had ordained with Abraham that He would take vengeance on them as they had brought them by force into bondage. (48:8).
And the prince Mastêmâ stood up against you, and sought to cast you into the hands of Pharaoh, and he helped the Egyptian sorcerers, (48:9).
and they stood up and wrought before you the evils indeed we permitted them to work, but the remedies we did not allow to be wrought by their hands. (48:10).
And the Lord smote them with malignant ulcers, and they were not able to stand, for we destroyed them so that they could not perform a single sign. (48:11).

And notwithstanding all (these) signs and wonders the prince Mastêmâ was not put to shame because he took courage and cried to the Egyptians to pursue after you with all the powers of the Egyptians, with their chariots, and with their horses, and with all the hosts of the peoples of Egypt. (48:12).

And I stood between the Egyptians and Israel, and we delivered Israel out of his hand, and out of the hand of his people, and the Lord brought them through the midst of the sea as if it were dry land. (48:13).

And all the peoples whom he brought to pursue after Israel, the Lord our God cast them into the midst of the sea, into the depths of the abyss beneath the children of Israel, even as the people of Egypt had cast their children into the river He took vengeance on 1,000,000 of them, and one thousand strong and energetic men were destroyed on account of one suckling of the children of your people which they had thrown into the river. (48:14).

And on the fourteenth day and on the fifteenth and on the sixteenth and on the seventeenth and on the eighteenth the prince Mastêmâ was bound and imprisoned behind the children of Israel that he might not accuse them. (48:15).
And on the nineteenth we let them loose that they might help the Egyptians and pursue the children of Israel. (48:16).
And he hardened their hearts and made them stubborn, and the device was devised by the Lord our God that He might smite the Egyptians and cast them into the sea. (48:17).

And on the fourteenth we bound him that he might not accuse the children of Israel on the day when they asked the Egyptians for vessels and garments, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and vessels of bronze, in order to despoil the Egyptians in return for the bondage in which they had forced them to serve. (48:18).
And we did not lead forth the children of Israel from Egypt empty handed. (48:19).
crossRefs: Exodus 4:24-26: The LORD meets Moses at the lodging place on the way and seeks to kill him, until Zipporah cuts off her son's foreskin and touches his feet with it.
Exodus 7:8-13: Aaron's rod becomes a serpent, the magicians of Egypt do the same by their enchantments, and Aaron's rod swallows up theirs.
Exodus 9:8-11: Ashes thrown toward heaven become boils breaking out in sores on man and beast, and the magicians cannot stand before Moses because the boils are on them too.
Exodus 12:35-36: Israel asks the Egyptians for jewels of silver and gold and for garments, and the LORD gives them favour, so that they spoil the Egyptians.
Exodus 14:19-31: The angel of God moves between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel, the sea goes back all night, Israel walks through on dry ground and the waters return over the chariots.

translationNotes.note: At 48:2-4 the book says the prince Mastema tried with all his power to kill Moses on the road back into Egypt, and that the angel delivered him. Exodus 4:24-26 tells the same episode very differently: the LORD met him and sought to kill him, and the danger passed when Zipporah circumcised their son. The book names Mastema as the attacker; Exodus does not.

The chartummim are Egypt's ritual specialists, the men trained in the sacred writings and the temple rites; the same word covers the Babylonian experts at Daniel 2:2. At 48:9-11 Mastema helps them so they can copy the signs but never the cures, until the ulcers put them out of action altogether, which is what Exodus 9:11 records.

translationNotes.term: Bound from the fourteenth to the eighteenth
translationNotes.note: At 48:15-18 Mastema is shut up over the days from the fourteenth of the first month, which is Passover, through the eighteenth, so that he cannot accuse Israel while they are asking the Egyptians for silver and gold, then loosed on the nineteenth to drive the pursuit. Exodus 12:29-51 covers the same days and mentions no accuser at all.

At 48:18-19 Israel asks for vessels of silver, gold and bronze and for garments, and the book says outright that this is payment in return for the bondage they were forced to serve. Exodus 3:21-22 promises it in advance and Exodus 12:35-36 records it happening. Deuteronomy 15:13-14 requires the same of any Israelite freeing a slave: do not send him away empty.

At 48:14 the book puts the Egyptian dead in the sea at a million, and reckons a thousand strong men lost for every one nursing child thrown into the river. Exodus 14:28 says the waters covered the chariots and the horsemen and all the host of Pharaoh without giving a number, and Exodus 14:7 counts six hundred chosen chariots in the pursuit.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses is in Midian, then returns, and Mastema tries to kill him on the road at the lodging place. The ten plagues fall, Mastema backs the sorcerers until the ulcers stop them, and he is bound from the fourteenth to the eighteenth so he cannot accuse Israel, then loosed to drive the pursuit.

stories.title: 📜 Jubilees 49
summaryBullets: Remember the commandment which the Lord commanded you concerning the passover, that you should celebrate it in its season on the fourteenth of the first month, that you should kill it before it is evening, and that they should eat it by night on the evening of the fifteenth from the time of the setting of the sun. (49:1).

For on this night -the beginning of the festival and the beginning of the joy- you were eating the passover in Egypt, when all the powers of Mastêmâ had been let loose to slay all the first-born in the land of Egypt, from the first-born of Pharaoh to the first-born of the captive maid-servant in the mill, and to the cattle. (49:2).

And this is the sign which the Lord gave them: Into every house on the lintels of which they saw the blood of a lamb of the first year, into (that) house they should not enter to slay, but should pass by (it), that all those should be saved that were in the house because the sign of the blood was on its lintels. (49:3).

And the powers of the Lord did everything according as the Lord commanded them, and they passed by all the children of Israel, and the plague came not upon them to destroy from amongst them any soul either of cattle, or man, or dog. (49:4).
And the plague was very grievous in Egypt, and there was no house in Egypt where there was not one dead, and weeping and lamentation. (49:5).

And all Israel was eating the flesh of the paschal lamb, and drinking the wine, and was lauding, and blessing, and giving thanks to the Lord God of their fathers, and was ready to go forth from under the yoke of Egypt, and from the evil bondage. (49:6).

And remember you this day all the days of your life, and observe it from year to year all the days of your life, once a year, on its day, according to all the law thereof, and do not adjourn (it) from day to day, or from month to month. (49:7).

For it is an eternal ordinance, and engraven on the heavenly tablets regarding all the children of Israel that they should observe it every year on its day once a year, throughout all their generations; and there is no limit of days, for this is ordained for ever. (49:8).

And the man who is free from uncleanness, and does not come to observe it on occasion of its day, so as to bring an acceptable offering before the Lord, and to eat and to drink before the Lord on the day of its festival, that man who is clean and close at hand shall be cut off: because he offered not the oblation of the Lord in its appointed season, he shall take the guilt upon himself. (49:9).

Let the children of Israel come and observe the passover on the day of its fixed time, on the fourteenth day of the first month, between the evenings, from the third part of the day to the third part of the night, for two portions of the day are given to the light, and a third part to the evening. (49:10).
This is that which the Lord commanded you that you should observe it between the evenings. (49:11).

And it is not permissible to slay it during any period of the light, but during the period bordering on the evening, and let them eat it at the time of the evening, until the third part of the night, and whatever is left over of all its flesh from the third part of the night and onwards, let them burn it with fire. (49:12).

And they shall not cook it with water, nor shall they eat it raw, but roast on the fire: they shall eat it with diligence, its head with the inwards thereof and its feet they shall roast with fire, and not break any bone thereof; for of the children of Israel no bone shall be crushed. (49:13).

For this reason the Lord commanded the children of Israel to observe the passover on the day of its fixed time, and they shall not break a bone thereof; for it is a festival day, and a day commanded, and there may be no passing over from day to day, and month to month, but on the day of its festival let it be observed. (49:14).

And do you command the children of Israel to observe the passover throughout their days, every year, once a year on the day of its fixed time, and it shall come for a memorial well pleasing before the Lord, and no plague shall come upon them to slay or to smite in that year in which they celebrate the passover in its season in every respect according to His command. (49:15).

And they shall not eat it outside the sanctuary of the Lord, but before the sanctuary of the Lord, and all the people of the congregation of Israel shall celebrate it in its appointed season. (49:16).

And every man who has come upon its day shall eat it in the sanctuary of your God before the Lord from twenty years old and upward; for thus is it written and ordained that they should eat it in the sanctuary of the Lord. (49:17).

And when the children of Israel come into the land which they are to possess, into the land of Canaan, and set up the tabernacle of the Lord in the midst of the land in one of their tribes until the sanctuary of the Lord has been built in the land, let them come and celebrate the passover in the midst of the tabernacle of the Lord, and let them slay it before the Lord from year to year. (49:18).

And in the days when the house has been built in the name of the Lord in the land of their inheritance, they shall go there and slay the passover in the evening, at sunset, at the third part of the day. (49:19).

And they shall offer its blood on the threshold of the altar, and shall place its fat on the fire which is upon the altar, and they shall eat its flesh roasted with fire in the court of the house which has been sanctified in the name of the Lord. (49:20).

And they may not celebrate the passover in their cities, nor in any place save before the tabernacle of the Lord, or before His house where His name has dwelt; and they shall not go astray from the Lord. (49:21).

And do you, Moses, command the children of Israel to observe the ordinances of the passover, as it was commanded to you; declare you to them every year and the day of its days, and the festival of unleavened bread, that they should eat unleavened bread seven days, (and) that they should observe its festival, and that they bring an oblation every day during those seven days of joy before the Lord on the altar of your God. (49:22).
For you celebrated this festival with haste when you went forth from Egypt till you entered into the wilderness of Shur; for on the shore of the sea you completed it. (49:23).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:1-14: The lamb taken on the tenth and killed on the fourteenth between the evenings, the blood struck on the two side posts and the lintel, the flesh roast with fire, and the LORD passing over.
Deuteronomy 16:5-7: You may not sacrifice the passover within any of your gates, but only at the place the LORD chooses to put His name, the rule this chapter presses hard.
Numbers 9:9-13: A man unclean or away on a journey keeps the passover a month later, but a man who is clean and at hand and does not keep it is cut off from his people.
Exodus 13:6-8: Seven days of unleavened bread with a feast on the seventh, and a father telling his son what the LORD did for him when he came out of Egypt.
John 19:36: These things were done so that the scripture should be fulfilled, a bone of him shall not be broken.

translationNotes.note: The phrase at Exodus 12:6 fixes when the lamb is killed, and it does not carry over into English. At 49:10-12 this book defines it in hours: from the third part of the day to the third part of the night, since two parts of the day belong to the light and one to the evening. The killing falls in that last third of daylight and the eating runs to the end of the first third of the night.

At 49:13 the lamb may not be boiled or eaten raw but must be roasted whole on the fire, head and legs and inwards together, which follows Exodus 12:8-9. Roasting it whole is what makes the rule against breaking a bone workable, since there is no jointing and no pot.

The mashqof is the beam across the top of a doorway and the doorposts are the uprights on either side. Exodus 12:7 has the blood struck on both posts and the lintel, and Exodus 12:22 says it was applied with a bunch of hyssop. At 49:3 the book mentions the lintels and calls the blood the sign that turned the destroyer aside.

At 49:17 only men of twenty and upward eat the Passover at the sanctuary. Twenty is the age of a counted man elsewhere in Israel: Numbers 1:3 musters those from twenty years old and upward able to go to war, and Exodus 30:14 takes the half shekel from twenty upward. The law of Moses sets no minimum age for eating the Passover.

The desert strip east of Egypt on the way into Sinai. Exodus 15:22 has Israel go out into the wilderness of Shur after crossing the sea and travel three days without finding water. At 49:23 this book says the seven days of unleavened bread were finished on the shore of the sea as they reached it.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Passover is killed on the fourteenth of the first month before evening and eaten that night, and the blood on the lintels is the sign that kept Israel while the firstborn of Egypt died. The chapter fixes the hours, forbids boiling it or breaking a bone, and allows it eaten only at the sanctuary.

stories.title: 📜 Jubilees 50
summaryBullets: And after this law I made known to you the days of the Sabbaths in the desert of Sin[ai], which is between Elim and Sinai. (50:1).

And I told you of the Sabbaths of the land on Mount Sinai, and I told you of the jubilee years in the sabbaths of years: but the year thereof have I not told you till you enter the land which you are to possess. (50:2).
And the land also shall keep its sabbaths while they dwell upon it, and they shall know the jubilee year. (50:3).

Wherefore I have ordained for you the year-weeks and the years and the jubilees: there are forty-nine jubilees from the days of Adam until this day, [2410 A.M.] and one week and two years: and there are yet forty years to come (lit. 'distant') for learning the [2450 A.M.] commandments of the Lord, until they pass over into the land of Canaan, crossing the Jordan to the west. (50:4).

And the jubilees shall pass by, until Israel is cleansed from all guilt of fornication, and uncleanness, and pollution, and sin, and error, and dwells with confidence in all the land, and there shall be no more a Satan or any evil one, and the land shall be clean from that time for evermore. (50:5).
And behold the commandment regarding the Sabbaths -I have written (them) down for you- and all the judgments of its laws. (50:6).

Six days shalt you labour, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. In it you will do no manner of work, you and your sons, and your men- servants and your maid-servants, and all your cattle and the sojourner also who is with you. (50:7).

And the man that does any work on it shall die: whoever desecrates that day, whoever lies with (his) wife, or whoever says he will do something on it, that he will set out on a journey thereon in regard to any buying or selling: and whoever draws water thereon which he had not prepared for himself on the sixth day, and whoever takes up any burden to carry it out of his tent or out of his house shall die. (50:8).

You will do no work whatever on the Sabbath day save what you have prepared for yourselves on the sixth day, so as to eat, and drink, and rest, and keep Sabbath from all work on that day, and to bless the Lord your God, who has given you a day of festival and a holy day: and a day of the holy kingdom for all Israel is this day among their days for ever. (50:9).

For great is the honour which the Lord has given to Israel that they should eat and drink and be satisfied on this festival day, and rest thereon from all labour which belongs to the labour of the children of men save burning frankincense and bringing oblations and sacrifices before the Lord for days and for Sabbaths. (50:10).

This work alone shall be done on the Sabbath-days in the sanctuary of the Lord your God; that they may atone for Israel with sacrifice continually from day to day for a memorial well-pleasing before the Lord, and that He may receive them always from day to day according as you have been commanded. (50:11).

And every man who does any work thereon, or goes a journey, or tills (his) farm, whether in his house or any other place, and whoever lights a fire, or rides on any beast, or travels by ship on the sea, and whoever strikes or kills anything, or slaughters a beast or a bird, or whoever catches an animal or a bird or a fish, or whoever fasts or makes war on the Sabbaths: (50:12).

The man who does any of these things on the Sabbath shall die, so that the children of Israel shall observe the Sabbaths according to the commandments regarding the Sabbaths of the land, as it is written in the tablets, which He gave into my hands that I should write out for you the laws of the seasons, and the seasons according to the division of their days. Herewith is completed the account of the division of the days. (50:13).
crossRefs: Leviticus 25:1-13: The land keeps its sabbaths every seventh year, seven sabbaths of years make forty-nine, and the fiftieth is hallowed as a jubilee with liberty proclaimed through all the land.
Exodus 20:8-11: Remember the sabbath day to keep it holy, six days of labour and the seventh a rest for you, your household, your servants, your cattle and the stranger inside your gates.
Exodus 35:2-3: Whoever does work on the sabbath day shall be put to death, and no fire shall be kindled in any dwelling on that day.
Numbers 15:32-36: A man is found gathering sticks on the sabbath, is held in custody until the sentence is given, and is then stoned by the whole congregation.
Nehemiah 13:15-22: Nehemiah finds men treading winepresses and hauling loads into Jerusalem on the sabbath, and has the gates shut from dusk until the day is over.

translationNotes.note: At 50:4 the book totals its own chronology: forty-nine jubilees plus one week plus two years from Adam to the giving of the law, which is 2401 plus seven plus two, or 2410 years, with forty more before Israel crosses the Jordan. That brings creation to the land at fifty jubilees exactly, 2450 years, and the whole book is built to fill that frame.

Leviticus 25:8-13 counts seven sabbaths of years, forty-nine of them, then hallows the fiftieth with the horn sounded on the day of atonement: slaves go free, land returns to the family that lost it, and nobody sows or reaps. At 50:2-3 the angel says he has told Moses the sabbaths of the land and the jubilee years but not the current count, which waits until they are in the land.

At 50:8 and 50:12 the book lists acts that carry death on the sabbath: working, drawing water not prepared the day before, carrying a burden out of house or tent, buying and selling, planning a journey, lighting a fire, riding a beast, sailing, slaughtering, hunting, fasting, and making war. Exodus 35:3 forbids kindling fire and Exodus 16:23-29 covers the water and food prepared in advance; the rest of the list is this book's.

At 50:12 making war on the sabbath sits among the capital offences. That rule had a hard history: 1 Maccabees 2:29-38 records about a thousand people killed in the caves because they would not fight on the sabbath, and 1 Maccabees 2:39-41 records the decision taken afterwards to fight back if attacked on that day.

At 50:1 the sabbath laws are given in the desert of Sin, between Elim and Sinai. Exodus 16:1 places Israel there on the fifteenth day of the second month, and it is where the manna begins, with a double portion gathered on the sixth day and none falling on the seventh, Exodus 16:22-30. That is the setting in which the sabbath is first taught to the people.

stories.keyTakeaway: The angel closes with the sabbaths given in the wilderness of Sin and states the book's own chronology: forty-nine jubilees, one week and two years from Adam to this day, with forty years still to run. He then lists what is forbidden on the sabbath, and says the man who does those things dies.

intro:
Jubilees presents its contents as revelation given to Moses on Mount Sinai. It opens with a date: the first year of the exodus from Egypt, the third month, the sixteenth day, when God calls Moses up the mountain and gives him the tables of stone (1:1-4). God then tells the angel of the presence, "Write for Moses from the beginning of creation till My sanctuary has been built among them for all eternity" (1:26). From chapter 2 to the end, that angel is the speaker, and Moses is the man he is speaking to. The book names no later author. The fifty chapters retell Genesis from creation through the death of Joseph, then Exodus down to the Passover and the departure from Egypt, and close with the sabbath laws given in the wilderness of Sin (50:1-13). The retelling is dated throughout. History is measured in jubilee periods of forty-nine years, each made of seven weeks of seven years, and every event is fixed within one: Cain is born in the third week of the second jubilee, Abel in the fourth (4:1). The chronology closes its own circle at 50:4, which counts forty-nine jubilees from the days of Adam to the giving of the law, plus one week and two years, with forty years still to run before Israel crosses the Jordan. That totals fifty jubilees, two thousand four hundred and fifty years from creation to the land. Alongside the chronology the book carries material Genesis does not: the names of the wives of the patriarchs, Enoch as the first man who learned writing and wrote down the signs of heaven (4:17-19), the angels who came down in the days of Jared, the demonic prince Mastema, and laws written on the heavenly tablets before they were given at Sinai.

The calendar is the feature a reader most needs explained. Jubilees requires a year of three hundred and sixty-four days and nothing else: "command the children of Israel that they observe the years according to this reckoning, three hundred and sixty-four days, and these will constitute a complete year" (6:32). The structure is four seasons of thirteen weeks each, fifty-two weeks exactly (6:29-30), with the new moons of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months kept as days of remembrance at the four divisions of the year (6:23). Because 364 divides evenly by seven, every date falls on the same day of the week every year and no appointed feast can drift onto a sabbath. The book states the consequence of abandoning it directly: Israel will forget the path of the years, will confound the new moons, seasons, sabbaths, and festivals, and those who reckon by the moon will run ten days early (6:33-38).

The book carries several names. Greek writers called it Leptogenesis, the Little Genesis, the minutiae of Genesis; Epiphanius uses that title when he cites it in the Panarion (39.6, c. AD 375), and George Syncellus quotes it around AD 810. Its Ge'ez name is Kufale, the Book of Divisions. The Damascus Document found at Qumran cites it by a fuller form of the same title, the Book of the Divisions of the Times into their Jubilees and Weeks (CD 16:2-4), which matches the book's own prologue. Jubilees was composed in Hebrew. Roughly fifteen copies were recovered from five caves at Qumran, all Hebrew, more copies than survive there for most books of the Hebrew Bible; the oldest, 4Q216, is dated by its script to about 125 BC, and the Damascus Document that cites it is dated near 100 BC, so the book was written and in authoritative use before then. The complete text survives only in Ge'ez, in twenty-seven or so manuscripts of the fifteenth century and later. August Dillmann published a German translation in 1850-51 and the Ge'ez text in 1859 as Kufale sive Liber Jubilaeorum; R. H. Charles published the Ethiopic text in 1895 and an English translation in 1902. A Latin translation survives in part, deciphered from a fifth or sixth century palimpsest in the Ambrosian Library at Milan and published by Antonio Maria Ceriani in 1861. A Syriac witness survives as a list in British Library Add. 12154 headed with the names of the wives of the patriarchs according to the Hebrew book called Jubilees, printed by Ceriani in the same year.

Jubilees is canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, where it stands in the Old Testament under the name Kufale, and in the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and it is received in the Haymanot tradition of the Beta Israel. No other communion receives it. It is not in the Jewish canon, not in the Septuagint or Vulgate collections received by the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, and not in the Protestant Bible or its Apocrypha.
